cl_aya_dmt_entities.short: Mostly a being, a guide, a spirit or an alien. 69 in 100 said it gave them a message. People who said they'd met God without drugs told similar stories.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.but: Only people who'd had such a meeting took part, so we can't tell how often it happens.
how: In 2018, 2,561 adults described their most memorable meeting with a being after smoking or vaping DMT. Looking back, 65 in 100 judged it more real than everyday life.
On DMT, most said the being seemed conscious, intelligent and kind. Still, 41 in 100 felt fear at some point.
Not just DMT: of 809 people who said they met God or a higher power without drugs, 86 in 100 called it kind and 78 in 100 said they got a message.
28 in 100 recalled being atheists before DMT, and 10 in 100 said they were now. Without drugs, the share fell too. But people recalled their old beliefs years later.
cl_aya_dmt_entities.rate: Two online surveys from one team, only of people who'd had such a meeting, looking back years later. They show what people believe, not how often this happens or whether the beings are real.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who said they met a being on DMT, in one survey:
pairs: said it gave them a message
freq.note: 2,561 adults recruited online in 2018, each describing their most memorable meeting after smoking or vaping DMT; only people who reported a meeting took part.

cl_aya_dmt_entities.note: Short answers first, with the freq's 69; scare quotes dropped; added how real it felt; rate says what surveys can't show.

cl_mdma_response_predictors.short: Yes. The biggest link was the amount per kilo of body weight: given the same amount, lighter people got more per kilo, which went with stronger effects.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.but: That's one lab's healthy young volunteers in a hospital, most trying MDMA for the first time.
how: 194 healthy young adults took MDMA in hospital, one set amount each time. On another day they took a dummy pill.
The amount per kilo of body weight went most with how strong it felt. Women and men didn't clearly differ once weight was counted, though an earlier report suggested women may feel more bad effects.
People who tend to worry, or who felt anxious and low just before, said they felt more anxious than calm people did. Open people felt closer to others.
Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.rate: Ten pooled studies from one lab, with 194 healthy volunteers. It compares people who differ in many ways, so it shows links, not causes, and each link was modest.
cl_mdma_response_predictors.note: Short opens with Yes and the weight finding; How 2 trimmed to length; rate keeps only what the claim states.

cl_meth_acute_toxicity.q: What does a meth overdose look like?
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.short: A meth overdose can look like a body in overdrive: a racing heart, fast breathing, being very restless and upset. Some people lose touch with reality.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.but: That's second-hand, from two reviews of hospital studies, and how often each sign shows up varies a lot.
how: Signs include a racing heart, high blood pressure, fast breathing and wide pupils. People can be very restless and upset.
The body can get very hot. Chest pain and organ failure can happen, and some people die.
One review found psychosis (losing touch with reality) in 12 to 80 in 100 people seen in hospital, and suicidal thoughts or acts in 6 to 50, depending on the study.
Neither review says how many patients die.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.rate: Two reviews of hospital records and case reports; the original studies could not be checked through them. Some of those studies were about amphetamine or other stimulants, not meth.
cl_meth_acute_toxicity.note: Question in people's words (overdose); mental signs added with their ranges; But plainer; How 4 given its sources.

cl_aya_ceremony_setting.short: A little. People who felt safer and better supported at their last ceremony recalled slightly less fear and fewer problems afterwards.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.but: One survey: people rated the ceremony and how it went at the same time, looking back.
how: Almost 7,000 people who had drunk ayahuasca answered one online survey about their last ceremony.
Each step up on a 1-to-4 rating of feeling safe and supported went with about 0.3 points less fear, out of 10, and slightly fewer problems in the weeks after.
More traditional practices, and drinking in Amazon countries other than Brazil, went with more fear; church hymns or sermons with less.
Fasting showed no link the study could detect with fear or later problems. All the differences were small, and nothing was measured before people drank.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.rate: One large survey, recruited through the groups whose ceremonies were rated. People rated the ceremony and how it went at the same sitting, looking back, so each answer could colour the other.
cl_aya_ceremony_setting.note: Short now opens with the direct answer; How 2 gives the claim's size in plain numbers.

cl_xc_setting_support.short: Maybe a little. In surveys, people who felt safe and supported reported slightly fewer hard moments.
cl_xc_setting_support.but: People rated this looking back; the one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips, but the link was weak and could be chance.
Among almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear than others.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, to compare them. A review of 25 trials found none either; some used plain hospital rooms, others disguised them as living rooms.
cl_xc_setting_support.rate: Four studies, mostly surveys of people who chose to answer and rated everything afterwards. Results differ by what was asked: blaming the people around showed no link with how hard trips were.
cl_xc_setting_support.note: Short opens with the direct answer instead of the study; How 4 cut to length.

cl_can_legal_teens.short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.
cl_can_legal_teens.but: Just 7 states had surveys from both before and after the change, and only for its first few years.
how: Surveys gathered 1.4 million answers from US high school students, 1993 to 2017. Each state was compared before and after its law, against other states.
After recreational laws, the odds of past-month cannabis use were 8% lower. That is not 8 fewer teens in 100, but at most about 2.
Laws for medical cannabis, in 27 states and Washington, DC, were not linked to teen use either way, once other things were counted.
The authors suggest shops that check age make cannabis harder for teens to get. Their source: a 2012 news article. The study didn't test it.
cl_can_legal_teens.rate: Surveys in US schools, not a fair test. Only 7 states had legal cannabis with surveys before and after, no one checked if they were already changing, and other studies were mixed.
cl_can_legal_teens.note: No change: already answers first, plainly, with the honest catch.

cl_opi_poppy_seeds.short: Yes, it can. In one study, all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine in their urine above the sports limit of the time.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.but: The cake used the strongest of 8 seed products tested. It had about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the rest.
how: Researchers in Germany tested 8 poppy seed products from shops and a bakery. All held some morphine; one held far more than the rest.
9 volunteers ate cake made with that one. Every person's urine went over the sports limit in at least 2 samples.
One of the 9 was still above the limit about 2 days later; the other 8 had their last positive within a day.
Only the sports limit was checked; workplace tests were not studied. A positive is a urine result, not a measure of any effect.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.rate: One small study: 9 volunteers, one very morphine-rich batch of seeds, no comparison cake and no urine sample before eating. Workplace tests were not checked.
cl_opi_poppy_seeds.note: Short opens with Yes, not the study; says the limit was the one used then, as the claim does.

cl_dc_nitazene_strips.short: Mostly, in the lab. They picked up 24 of 33 kinds of nitazene but missed most desnitazenes, so a negative doesn't rule nitazenes out.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.but: Only pure or nearly pure drugs were tested. Mixed street drugs were not.
how: One lab tried 33 kinds of nitazene. The strips picked up 24. They missed 6 of the 7 desnitazenes, even at high strength.
Six nearly pure powders from the drug market all showed up.
A second lab found the strips did not react to 76 other drugs and cutting agents.
No study we read tested street drugs where a nitazene is a small part of a mix, so how often strips get it wrong on real samples is unknown.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.rate: Two labs tested one brand of strip on pure or nearly pure samples in water, not messy street drugs. Most kinds of nitazene were tested with just one strip per strength.
cl_dc_nitazene_strips.note: Short answers first with the count and the authors' point on negatives; How 4 hedged as the claim is, sourced.

cl_ket_depression_infusion.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it hard to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after a ketamine drip. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.
cl_ket_depression_infusion.rate: Many trials agree, but people could often tell they got ketamine. Trials that found nothing may also be missing.

freq.what: were much better a day after one ketamine drip
freq.note: One trial at two US research centres, 2010 to 2012: 30 of 47 given ketamine and 7 of 25 given midazolam.

cl_ket_depression_infusion.note: Short now opens with the direct answer; same 64 and 28 as the picture.

cl_mdma_therapy_contested.short: It's not settled. Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but can't show how much was the drug itself, or for how long.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.but: One sponsor ran both trials, and in the one that asked, most people knew their pill.
how: Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA and therapy than with a dummy pill and the same therapy; none tested MDMA against usual talking therapy.
But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected.
The company's own later check found the gap lasted, but the regulator said it wasn't built to show that; about 3 in 10 weren't checked and some knew their pill.
In 2024 the US regulator said no, after its advisers voted 9 to 2 that it wasn't shown to work. Three earlier studies were withdrawn for not disclosing rule-breaking at one site.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.rate: Two trials, where people often knew their pill and rated their own symptoms, and neither compared MDMA with existing therapy or looked beyond 18 weeks. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.
cl_mdma_therapy_contested.note: Short answers first and says why it's unsettled; How 3-4 add the regulator's view and the 9-to-2 vote.

cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.but: The trial was too small to show they work equally well, and people expected nearly twice as much from psilocybin.
how: At one London centre, 59 adults with depression got two psilocybin sessions, or 6 weeks of escitalopram pills plus two tiny psilocybin doses.
After 6 weeks, self-rated depression fell 8 points with psilocybin and 6 with escitalopram, on a 27-point scale: a gap that could be chance.
At 6 weeks, 57 in 100 were nearly free of symptoms with psilocybin and 28 with escitalopram, an extra result the authors drew no conclusions from. Six months on: 37 against 34.
People had higher hopes for psilocybin. Allowing for those hopes, the team found no clear gap on any of six scales.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.rate: One small trial of 59 people: too few to tell whether psilocybin and escitalopram work equally well. People rated their own depression, expected more from psilocybin, and by 6 months most had other treatment.
cl_psi_vs_escitalopram.note: No change: already answers first (not shown) in plain words, with the main catch.

cl_gen_stigma_health_care.short: Many health workers said they felt negative. Whether care was worse is not clear.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.but: Mostly surveys of what workers said, from 2000 to 2011, in a few countries.
how: A review gathered 28 studies, mostly from Australia, the UK and the US. In them, health workers described their views of patients with drug or alcohol problems.

Many workers felt negative about these patients, or less positive than about people with other illnesses. This was more common outside drug and alcohol services. Some studies found neutral or positive views.
Only a few studies asked whether this changes care, and they disagreed. In one, people who felt staff treated them unfairly were less likely to finish treatment.
In another, doctors' views were not linked to what patients said about their care. The one study that watched real visits, from the 1980s, found better care for these patients.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.rate: One review of 28 papers, mostly surveys of what health workers said, answered by those who chose to. We know them only through the review, whose summaries contain errors.
cl_gen_stigma_health_care.note: No change: already answers first and plainly, with the honest catch.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.q: How fast can you get hooked on cocaine?
cl_coc_dependence_onset.short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.
cl_coc_dependence_onset.but: People answered once, about themselves. The survey cannot show that crack itself made the difference.
how: US surveys from 2002 to 2016 asked people who had first used cocaine less than a year before.
About 5 in 100 of those who had used only powder met the criteria for cocaine dependence, and about 22 in 100 of those who had gone on to crack.
In both groups the most common problem was wanting or trying to cut down or stop: about 45 in 100 and 58 in 100.
People who go on to crack may differ to begin with, and some may already have had problems with powder. The survey did not ask which form caused a problem.
cl_coc_dependence_onset.rate: Yearly US surveys from 2002–2016. Only 275 people went on to crack, too few to be sure, and the two groups may have differed before they ever started.

freq.title: Out of every 100 people who had started cocaine in the past year, how many met the criteria for dependence?
pairs: people who had used only powder
people who had also gone on to crack
freq.note: US household surveys, 2002 to 2016. People were asked once, less than a year after they first used cocaine.

cl_coc_dependence_onset.note: Question in people's words (how_people_ask: how fast people get hooked); lines already plain, kept.

cl_mdma_acute_body.short: One dose pushes all three up. In lab tests, 24 in 100 people went over 38 degrees after MDMA, against 9 in 100 after a dummy pill.
cl_mdma_acute_body.but: Healthy volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees; heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses weren't tested.
how: In 136 healthy adults given one laboratory dose, the top blood-pressure number went above 160 in 38 in 100 after MDMA, against 6 in 100 after a dummy pill.
A heart rate above 100 happened in 33 in 100 after MDMA, against 2 in 100 after the dummy pill.
Ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 after MDMA, against 9 in 100; the highest was 39.1 degrees.
Four people felt no effect and the study does not say what their bodies did. Everyone got a set dose, so taking more was not tested here.
cl_mdma_acute_body.rate: Nine trials in one Basel lab compared MDMA with dummy pills in the same people, 166 healthy volunteers in all, and machines recorded large changes. But most people could probably tell when they had MDMA.
cl_mdma_acute_body.note: Short opens with the answer and a count; But gives the room's temperature, which 'cool' overstated.

cl_mdma_overheating.short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
cl_mdma_overheating.but: This is second-hand, from one review of small studies that could not tell heat, dancing and crowds apart.
how: In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose about 0.4 degrees on average at medium doses and 0.7 at higher ones; one person in a group of 8 went up 1.9.
At clubs and parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees, but the review reports no comparison of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowds, so which matters is unknown.

Severe overheating (40 degrees and up, sometimes fatal) is known from hospital cases. In one UK report, blood levels didn't suggest high doses; in another case, a friend who took the same MDMA didn't overheat.
People also feel it differently: in one survey, 16 in 100 people who take ecstasy did not feel hot.
cl_mdma_overheating.rate: One overview of small lab and party studies (4 to 41 people) and hospital cases. Each party study used a different comparison, or none, and their results differ widely without explanation.
cl_mdma_overheating.note: Two party points merged; added severe overheating from hospital cases, which answers the question asked.
